entries.3083a711ef4a38c08937f61c9e6a706d8900b6b8: <div sID="gen2853" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="11" osisID="Num.11" sID="Num.11"/> <div eID="gen2853" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2854" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen2855" type="x-p"/> Hitherto things had gone pretty well in Israel; little interruption had been given to the methods of God's favour to them since the matter of the golden calf; the people seemed teachable in marshalling and purifying the camp, the princes devout and generous in dedicating the altar, and there was good hope that they would be in Canaan presently. But at this chapter begins a melancholy scene; the measures are all broken, God has turned to be their enemy, and fights against them—and it is sin that makes all this mischief. I. Their murmurings kindled a fire among them, which yet was soon quenched by the prayer of Moses, <reference osisRef="Num.11.1-Num.11.3">ver. 1-3</reference>. II. No sooner was the fire of judgment quenched than the fire of sin breaks out again, and God takes occasion from it to magnify both his mercy and his justice. 1. The people fret for want of flesh, <reference osisRef="Num.11.4-Num.11.9">ver. 4-9</reference>. 2. Moses frets for want of help, <reference osisRef="Num.11.10-Num.11.15">ver. 10-15</reference>. Now, (1.) God promises to gratify them both, to appoint help for Moses (<reference osisRef="Num.11.16-Num.11.17">ver. 16, 17</reference>), and to give the people flesh, <reference osisRef="Num.11.18-Num.11.23">ver. 18-23</reference>. And, (2.) He presently makes good both these promises. For, [1.] The Spirit of God qualifies the seventy elders for the government, <reference osisRef="Num.11.24-Num.11.30">ver. 24-30</reference>. [2.] The power of God brings quails to feast the people, <reference osisRef="Num.11.31-Num.11.32">ver. 31, 32</reference>. Yet [3.] The justice of God plagued them for their murmurings, <reference osisRef="Num.11.33-Num.11.35">ver. 33</reference>, &c.
entries.91d1e1b6366e779f32b703a498e2d49b7a85edc1: <div eID="gen2855" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen2854" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Murmurings of the Israelites. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1490.)</title> <div sID="gen2856" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And <hi type="italic">when</hi> the people complained, it displeased the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : and the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> heard <hi type="italic">it;</hi> and his anger was kindled; and the fire of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> burnt among them, and consumed <hi type="italic">them that were</hi> in the uttermost parts of the camp. <hi type="super">2</hi> And the people cried unto Moses; and when Moses prayed unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , the fire was quenched. <hi type="super">3</hi> And he called the name of the place Taberah: because the fire of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> burnt among them. <div eID="gen2856" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2857" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. The people's sin. They <hi type="italic">complained,</hi> <reference osisRef="Num.11.1">v. 1</reference>. <hi type="italic">They were, as it were, complainers.</hi> So it is in the margin. There were some secret grudgings and discontents among them, which as yet did not break out in an open mutiny. But how great a matter did this little fire kindle! They had received from God excellent laws and ordinances, and yet no sooner had they departed from the mount of the Lord than they began to quarrel with God himself. See in this, 1. The sinfulness of sin, which takes occasion from the commandment to be the more provoking. 2. The weakness of the law through the flesh, <reference osisRef="Rom.8.3">Rom. viii. 3</reference>. The law discovered sin, but could not destroy it; checked it, but could not conquer it. They <hi type="italic">complained.</hi> Interpreters enquire what they complained of; and truly, when they were furnished with so much matter for thanksgiving, one may justly wonder where they found any matter for complaint; it is probable that those who complained did not all agree in the cause. Some perhaps complained that they were removed from Mount Sinai, where they had been at rest so long, others that they did not remove sooner: some complained of the weather, others of the ways: some perhaps thought three days' journey was too long a march, others thought it not long enough, because it did not bring them into Canaan. When we consider how their camp was guided, guarded, graced, what good victuals they had and good company, and what care was taken of them in their marches that their feet should not swell nor their clothes wear (<reference osisRef="Deut.8.4">Deut. viii. 4</reference>), we may ask, "What could have been done more for a people to make them easy?" And yet they complained. Note, Those that are of a fretful discontented spirit will always find something or other to quarrel with, though the circumstances of their outward condition be ever so favourable. <div eID="gen2857" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2858" type="x-p"/> II. God's just resentment of the affront given to him by this sin: <hi type="italic">The Lord heard it,</hi> though it does not appear that Moses did. Note, God is acquainted with the secret frettings and murmurings of the heart, though they are industriously concealed from men. What he took notice of his was much displeased with, and his <hi type="italic">anger was kindled.</hi> Note, Though God graciously gives us leave to complain to him when there is cause (<reference osisRef="Ps.142.2">Ps. cxlii. 2</reference>), yet he is justly provoked, and takes it very ill, if we complain of him when there is no cause: such conduct in our inferiors provokes us. <div eID="gen2858" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2859" type="x-p"/> III. The judgment wherewith God chastised them for this sin: <hi type="italic">The fire of the Lord burnt among them,</hi> such flashes of fire from the cloud as had consumed Nadab and Abihu. The fire of their wrath against God burned in their minds (<reference osisRef="Ps.39.3">Ps. xxxix. 3</reference>), and justly does the fire of God's wrath fasten upon their bodies. We read of their murmurings several times, when they came first out of Egypt, <reference osisRef="Exod.15.1-Exod.17.16">Exod. xv., and xvi., and xvii.</reference>. But we do not read of any plagues inflicted on them for their murmurings, as there were now; for now they had had great experience of God's care of them, and therefore now to distrust him was so much the more inexcusable. Now a <hi type="italic">fire was kindled against Jacob</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.78.21">Ps. lxxviii. 21</reference>), but, to show how unwilling God was to contend with them, it fastened on those only that were <hi type="italic">in the uttermost parts of the camp.</hi> Thus God's judgments came upon them gradually, that they might take warning. <div eID="gen2859" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2860" type="x-p"/> IV. Their cry to Moses, who was their tried intercessor, <reference osisRef="Num.11.2">v. 2</reference>. <hi type="italic">When he slew them, then they sought him,</hi> and made their application to Moses to stand their friend. Note, 1. When we complain without cause, it is just with God to give us cause to complain. 2. Those that slight God's friends when they are in prosperity would be glad to make them their friends when they are in distress. <hi type="italic">Father Abraham, send Lazarus.</hi> <div eID="gen2860" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2861" type="x-p"/> V. The prevalency of Moses's intercession for them: <hi type="italic">When Moses prayed unto the Lord</hi> (he was always ready to stand in the gap to turn away the wrath of God) God had respect to him and his offering, and <hi type="italic">the fire was quenched.</hi> By this it appears that God delights not in punishing, for, when he has begun his controversy, he is soon prevailed with to let it fall. Moses was one of those worthies who <hi type="italic">by faith quenched the violence of fire.</hi> <div eID="gen2861" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2862" type="x-p"/> VI. A new name given hereupon to the place, to perpetuate the shame of a murmuring people and the honour of a righteous God; the place was called <hi type="italic">Taberah,</hi> a <hi type="italic">burning</hi> (<reference osisRef="Num.11.3">v. 3</reference>), that others might hear, and fear, and take warning not to sin as they did, lest they should smart as they did, <reference osisRef="1Cor.10.10">1 Cor. x. 10</reference>.
entries.745741d31f1e0d62affd9250efe61918cf21b72b: <div eID="gen2862" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2863" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">4</hi> And the mixt multitude that <hi type="italic">was</hi> among them fell a lusting: and the children of Israel also wept again, and said, Who shall give us flesh to eat? <hi type="super">5</hi> We remember the fish, which we did eat in Egypt freely; the cucumbers, and the melons, and the leeks, and the onions, and the garlick: <hi type="super">6</hi> But now our soul <hi type="italic">is</hi> dried away: <hi type="italic">there is</hi> nothing at all, beside this manna, <hi type="italic">before</hi> our eyes. <hi type="super">7</hi> And the manna <hi type="italic">was</hi> as coriander seed, and the colour thereof as the colour of bdellium. <hi type="super">8</hi> <hi type="italic">And</hi> the people went about, and gathered <hi type="italic">it,</hi> and ground <hi type="italic">it</hi> in mills, or beat <hi type="italic">it</hi> in a mortar, and baked <hi type="italic">it</hi> in pans, and made cakes of it: and the taste of it was as the taste of fresh oil. <hi type="super">9</hi> And when the dew fell upon the camp in the night, the manna fell upon it. <hi type="super">10</hi> Then Moses heard the people weep throughout their families, every man in the door of his tent: and the anger of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> was kindled greatly; Moses also was displeased. <hi type="super">11</hi> And Moses said unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , Wherefore hast thou afflicted thy servant? and wherefore have I not found favour in thy sight, that thou layest the burden of all this people upon me? <hi type="super">12</hi> Have I conceived all this people? have I begotten them, that thou shouldest say unto me, Carry them in thy bosom, as a nursing father beareth the sucking child, unto the land which thou swarest unto their fathers? <hi type="super">13</hi> Whence should I have flesh to give unto all this people? for they weep unto me, saying, Give us flesh, that we may eat. <hi type="super">14</hi> I am not able to bear all this people alone, because <hi type="italic">it is</hi> too heavy for me. <hi type="super">15</hi> And if thou deal thus with me, kill me, I pray thee, out of hand, if I have found favour in thy sight; and let me not see my wretchedness. <div eID="gen2863" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2864" type="x-p"/> These verses represent things sadly unhinged and out of order in Israel, both the people and the prince uneasy. <div eID="gen2864" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2865" type="x-p"/> I. Here is the people fretting, and speaking against God himself (as it is interpreted, <reference osisRef="Ps.78.19">Ps. lxxviii. 19</reference>), notwithstanding his glorious appearances both to them and for them. Observe, <div eID="gen2865" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2866" type="x-p"/> 1. Who were the criminals. (1.) The <hi type="italic">mixed multitude</hi> began, they <hi type="italic">fell a lusting,</hi> <reference osisRef="Num.11.4">v. 4</reference>. The rabble that came with them out of Egypt, expecting only the land of promise, but not a state of probation in the way to it. They were hangers on, who took hold of the skirts of the Jews, and would go with them only because they knew not how to live at home, and were disposed to seek their fortunes (as we say) abroad. These were the scabbed sheep that infected the flock, the leaven that leavened the whole lump. Note, A few factious, discontented, ill-natured people, may do a great deal of mischief in the best societies, if great care be not taken to discountenance them. Such as these are an <hi type="italic">untoward generation,</hi> from which it is our wisdom to <hi type="italic">save ourselves,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.2.40">Acts ii. 40</reference>. (2.) Even <hi type="italic">the children of Israel</hi> took the infection, as we are informed, <reference osisRef="Num.11.4">v. 4</reference>. The holy seed joined themselves to the people of these abominations. The mixed multitude here spoken of were not numbered with the children of Israel, but were set aside as a people God made no account of; and yet the children of Israel, forgetting their own character and distinction, herded themselves with them and learned their way, as if the scum and outcasts of the camp were to be the privy-counsellors of it. The children of Israel, a people near to God and highly privileged, yet drawn into rebellion against him! O how little honour has God in the world, when even the people which he formed for himself, to show forth his praise, were so much a dishonour to him! Therefore let none think that their external professions and privileges will be their security either against Satan's temptations to sin or God's judgments for sin. See <reference osisRef="1Cor.10.1-1Cor.10.2">1 Cor. x. 1, 2</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.10.12">12</reference>. <div eID="gen2866" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2867" type="x-p"/> 2. What was the crime: they lusted and murmured. Though they had been lately corrected for this sin, and many of them overthrown for it, as God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah, and the smell of the fire was still in their nostrils, yet they returned to it. See <reference osisRef="Prov.27.22">Prov. xxvii. 22</reference>. (1.) They magnified the plenty and dainties they had had in Egypt (<reference osisRef="Num.11.5">v. 5</reference>), as if God had done them a great deal of wrong in taking them thence. While they were in Egypt they sighed by reason of their burdens, for their lives were made bitter to them with hard bondage; and yet now they talk of Egypt as if they had all lived like princes there, when this serves as a colour for their present discontent. But with what face can they talk of eating fish in Egypt freely, or for nought, as if it cost them nothing, when they paid so dearly for it with their hard service? They <hi type="italic">remember the cucumbers, and the melons, and the leeks, and the onions, and the garlick</hi> (precious stuff indeed to be fond of!), but they do not remember the brick-kilns and the task-masters, the voice of the oppressor and the smart of the whip. No, these are forgotten by these ungrateful people. (2.) They were sick of the good provision God had made for them, <reference osisRef="Num.11.6">v. 6</reference>. It was bread from heaven, angels' food. To show how unreasonable their complaint was, it is here described, <reference osisRef="Num.11.7-Num.11.9">v. 7-9</reference>. It was good for food, and pleasant to the eye, every grain like an orient pearl; it was wholesome food and nourishing; it was not to be called <hi type="italic">dry bread,</hi> for it tasted like fresh oil; it was agreeable (the Jews say, <reference osisRef="Wis.16.20">Wisd. xvi. 20</reference>) to every man's palate, and tasted as he would have it; and, though it was still the same, yet, by the different ways of dressing it, it yielded them a grateful variety; it cost them no money, nor care, for it fell in the night, while they slept; and the labour of gathering it was not worth speaking of; they lived upon free quarter, and yet could talk of Egypt's cheapness and the fish they ate there freely. Nay, which was much more valuable than all this, the manna came from the immediate power and bounty of God, not from common providence, but from special favour. It was, as God's compassion, new every morning, always fresh, not as their food who live on shipboard. While they lived on manna, they seemed to be exempted from the curse which sin has brought on man, that in the <hi type="italic">sweat of his face should he eat bread.</hi> And yet they speak of manna with such scorn, as if it were not good enough to be meat for swine: <hi type="italic">Our soul is dried away.</hi> They speak as if God dealt hardly with them in allowing them no better food. At first they admired it (<reference osisRef="Exod.16.15">Exod. xvi. 15</reference>): <hi type="italic">What is this?</hi> "What a curious precious thing is this!" But now they despised it. Note, Peevish discontented minds will find fault with that which has no fault in it but that it is too good for them. It is very provoking to God to undervalue his favours, and to put a <hi type="italic">but</hi> upon our common mercies. Nothing but manna! Those that might be very happy often make themselves very miserable by their discontents. (3.) They could not be satisfied unless they had flesh to eat. They brought flocks and herds with them in great abundance out of Egypt; but either they were covetous, and could not find in their hearts to kill them, lest they should lessen their flocks (they must have flesh as cheap as they had bread, or they would not be pleased), or else they were curious, beef and mutton would not please them; they must have something more nice and delicate, like the fish they did eat in Egypt. Food would not serve; they must be feasted. They had feasted with God upon the peace-offerings which they had their share of; but it seems God did not keep a table good enough for them, they must have daintier bits than any that came to his altar. Note, It is an evidence of the dominion of the carnal mind when we are solicitous to have all the delights and satisfactions of sense wound up to the height of pleasurableness. <hi type="italic">Be not desirous of dainties,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.23.1-Prov.23.3">Prov. xxiii. 1-3</reference>. If God gives us food convenient, we ought to be thankful, though we do not eat the fat and drink the sweet. (4.) They distrusted the power and goodness of God as insufficient for their supply: <hi type="italic">Who will give us flesh to eat?</hi> taking it for granted that God could not. Thus this question is commented up on, <reference osisRef="Ps.78.19-Ps.78.20">Ps. lxxviii. 19, 20</reference>, <hi type="italic">Can he provide flesh also?</hi> though he had given them flesh with their bread once, when he saw fit (<reference osisRef="Exod.16.13">Exod. xvi. 13</reference>), and they might have expected that he would do it again, and in mercy, if, instead of murmuring, they had prayed. Note, It is an offence to God to let our desires go beyond our faith. (5.) They were eager and importunate in their desires; they <hi type="italic">lusted a lust,</hi> so the word is, lusted greatly and greedily, till they wept again for vexation. So childish were the children of Israel, and so humoursome, that they cried because they had not what they would have and when they would have it. They did not offer up this desire to God, but would rather be beholden to any one else than to him. We should not indulge ourselves in any desire which we cannot in faith turn into prayer, as we cannot when we <hi type="italic">ask meat for our lust,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.78.18">Ps. lxxviii. 18</reference>. For this sin the <hi type="italic">anger of the Lord was kindled greatly against them,</hi> which is written for our admonition, that we should not <hi type="italic">lust after evil things as they lusted,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.10.6">1 Cor. x. 6</reference>. (6.) Flesh is good food, and may lawfully be eaten; yet they are said to lust after evil things. What is lawful of itself becomes evil to us when it is what God does not allot to us and yet we eagerly desire it. <div eID="gen2867" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2868" type="x-p"/> II. Moses himself, though so meek and good a man, is uneasy upon this occasion: <hi type="italic">Moses also was displeased.</hi> Now, 1. It must be confessed that the provocation was very great. These murmurings of theirs reflected great dishonour upon God, and Moses laid to heart the reproaches cast on himself; they knew that he did his utmost for their good, and that he neither did nor could do any thing without a divine appointment; and yet to be thus continually teased and clamoured against by an unreasonable ungrateful people would break in upon the temper even of Moses himself. God considered this, and therefore we do not find that he chided him for his uneasiness. 2. Yet Moses expressed himself otherwise than became him upon this provocation, and came short of his duty both to God and Israel in these expostulations. (1.) He undervalues the honour God had put upon him, in making him the illustrious minister of his power and grace, in the deliverance and guidance of that peculiar people, which might have been sufficient to balance the burden. (2.) He complains too much of a sensible grievance, and lays too near his heart a little noise and fatigue. If he could not bear the toil of government, which was but running with the footman, how would he bear the terrors of war, which was contending with horses? He might easily have furnished himself with considerations enough to enable him to slight their clamours, and make nothing of them. (3.) He magnifies his own performances, that <hi type="italic">all the burden of the people lay upon him;</hi> whereas God himself did in effect ease him of all the burden. Moses needed not to be in care to provide quarters for them, or victuals; God did all. And, if any difficult case happened, he needed not to be in any perplexity, while he had the oracle to consult, and in it the divine wisdom to direct him, the divine authority to back him and bear him out, and almighty power itself to dispense rewards and punishments. (4.) He is not so sensible as he ought to be of the obligation he lay under, by virtue of the divine commission and command, to do the utmost he could for his people, when he suggests that because they were not the children of his body therefore he was not concerned to take a fatherly care of them, though God himself, who might employ him as he pleased, had appointed him to be a father to them. (5.) He takes too much to himself when he asks, <hi type="italic">Whence should I have flesh to give them</hi> (<reference osisRef="Num.11.13">v. 13</reference>), as if he were the housekeeper, and not God. <hi type="italic">Moses gave them not the bread,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.6.32">John vi. 32</reference>. Nor was it expected that he should give them the flesh, but as an instrument in God's hand; and if he meant, "Whence should God have it for them?" he too much limited the power of the Holy One of Israel. (6.) He speaks distrustfully of the divine grace when he despairs of being <hi type="italic">able to bear all this people,</hi> <reference osisRef="Num.11.14">v. 14</reference>. Had the work been much less, he could not have gone through it in his own strength; but had it been much greater, through God strengthening him, he might have done it. (7.) It was worst of all passionately to wish for death, and desire to be killed out of hand, because just at this time his life was made a little uneasy to him, <reference osisRef="Num.11.15">v. 15</reference>. Is this Moses? Is this the meekest of all the men on the earth? The best have their infirmities, and fail sometimes in the exercise of that grace for which they are most eminent. But God graciously overlooked Moses's passion at this time, and therefore we must not be severe in our animadversions upon it, but pray, <hi type="italic">Lord, lead us not into temptation.</hi>
entries.6256fe8a579bf431cccc3ec6b5078cdc71cbab16: <div eID="gen2868" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Assistance Provided for Moses. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1490.)</title> <div sID="gen2869" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">16</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> said unto Moses, Gather unto me seventy men of the elders of Israel, whom thou knowest to be the elders of the people, and officers over them; and bring them unto the tabernacle of the congregation, that they may stand there with thee. <hi type="super">17</hi> And I will come down and talk with thee there: and I will take of the spirit which <hi type="italic">is</hi> upon thee, and will put <hi type="italic">it</hi> upon them; and they shall bear the burden of the people with thee, that thou bear <hi type="italic">it</hi> not thyself alone. <hi type="super">18</hi> And say thou unto the people, Sanctify yourselves against to morrow, and ye shall eat flesh: for ye have wept in the ears of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , saying, Who shall give us flesh to eat? for <hi type="italic">it was</hi> well with us in Egypt: therefore the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> will give you flesh, and ye shall eat. 19 Ye shall not eat one day, nor two days, nor five days, neither ten days, nor twenty days; <hi type="super">20</hi> <hi type="italic">But</hi> even a whole month, until it come out at your nostrils, and it be loathsome unto you: because that ye have despised the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> which <hi type="italic">is</hi> among you, and have wept before him, saying, Why came we forth out of Egypt? <hi type="super">21</hi> And Moses said, The people, among whom I <hi type="italic">am,</hi> <hi type="italic">are</hi> six hundred thousand footmen; and thou hast said, I will give them flesh, that they may eat a whole month. <hi type="super">22</hi> Shall the flocks and the herds be slain for them, to suffice them? or shall all the fish of the sea be gathered together for them, to suffice them? 23 And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> said unto Moses, Is the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> 's hand waxed short? thou shalt see now whether my word shall come to pass unto thee or not. <div eID="gen2869" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2870" type="x-p"/> We have here God's gracious answer to both the foregoing complaints, wherein his goodness takes occasion from man's badness to appear so much the more illustrious. <div eID="gen2870" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2871" type="x-p"/> I. Provision is made for the redress of the grievances Moses complains of. If he find the weight of government lie too heavy upon him, though he was a little too passionate in his remonstrance, yet he shall be eased, not by being discarded from the government himself, as he justly might have been if God had been extreme to mark what he said amiss, but by having assistants appointed him, who should be, as the apostle speaks (<reference osisRef="1Cor.12.28">1 Cor. xii. 28</reference>), <hi type="italic">helps, governments</hi> (that is, helps in government), not at all to lesson or eclipse his honour, but to make the work more easy to him, and to <hi type="italic">bear the burden of the people with him.</hi> And that this provision might be both agreeable and really serviceable, <div eID="gen2871" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2872" type="x-p"/> 1. Moses is directed to nominate the persons, <reference osisRef="Num.11.16">v. 16</reference>. The people were too hot and heady and tumultuous to be entrusted with the election; Moses must please himself in the choice, that he may not afterwards complain. The number he is to choose is seventy men, according to the number of the souls that went down into Egypt. He must choose such as he knew to be elders, that is, wise and experienced men. Those that had acquitted themselves best, as <hi type="italic">rulers of thousands and hundreds</hi> (<reference osisRef="Exod.18.25">Exod. xviii. 25</reference>), purchase to themselves now this good degree. "Choose such as thou knowest to be elders indeed, and not in name only, officers that execute their office." We read of the same number of elders (<reference osisRef="Exod.24.1">Exod. xxiv. 1</reference>) that went up with Moses to Mount Sinai, but they were distinguished only for that occasion, these for a perpetuity; and, according to this constitution, the Sanhedrim, or great council of the Jews, which in after ages sat at Jerusalem, and was the highest court of judgment among them, consisted of seventy men. Our Saviour seems to have had an eye to it in the choice of seventy disciples, who were to be assistants to the apostles, <reference osisRef="Luke.10.1-Luke.10.24">Luke x.</reference> <div eID="gen2872" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2873" type="x-p"/> 2. God promises to qualify them. If they were not found fit for the employ, they should be made fit, else they might prove more a hindrance than a help to Moses, <reference osisRef="Num.11.17">v. 17</reference>. Though Moses had talked too boldly with God, yet God does not therefore break off communion with him; he bears a great deal with us, and we must with one another: <hi type="italic">I will come down</hi> (said God) <hi type="italic">and talk with thee,</hi> when thou art more calm and composed; <hi type="italic">and I will take of the same spirit</hi> of wisdom, and piety, and courage, <hi type="italic">that is upon thee,</hi> and <hi type="italic">put it upon them.</hi> Not that Moses had the less of the Spirit for their sharing, nor that they were hereby made equal with him; Moses was still unequalled (<reference osisRef="Deut.34.10">Deut. xxxiv. 10</reference>), but they were clothed with a spirit of government proportionable to their place, and with a spirit of prophecy to prove their divine call to it, the government being a Theocracy. Note, (1.) Those whom God employs in any service he qualifies for it, and those that are not in some measure qualified cannot think themselves duly called. (2.) All good qualifications are from God; every <hi type="italic">perfect gift is from the Father of lights.</hi> <div eID="gen2873" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2874" type="x-p"/> II. Even the humour of the discontented people shall be gratified too, that every mouth may be stopped. They are ordered to <hi type="italic">sanctify themselves</hi> (<reference osisRef="Num.11.18">v. 18</reference>), that is, to put themselves into a posture to receive such a proof of God's power as should be a token both of mercy and judgment. <hi type="italic">Prepare to meet thy God, O Israel,</hi> <reference osisRef="Amos.4.12">Amos iv. 12</reference>. <div eID="gen2874" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2875" type="x-p"/> 1. God promises (shall I say?)—he threatens rather, that they shall have their fill of flesh, that for a month together they shall not only be fed, but feasted, with flesh, besides their daily manna; and, if they have not a better government of their appetites than now it appears they have they shall be surfeited with it (<reference osisRef="Num.11.19-Num.11.20">v. 19, 20</reference>): You shall eat <hi type="italic">till it come out at your nostrils, and become loathsome to you.</hi> See here, (1.) The vanity of all the delights of sense; they will cloy, but not satisfy: spiritual pleasures are the contrary. As the world passes away, so do the lusts of it, <reference osisRef="1John.2.17">1 John ii. 17</reference>. What was greedily coveted in a little time comes to be nauseated. (2.) What brutish sins (and worse than brutish) gluttony and drunkenness are; they put a force upon nature, and make that the sickness of the body which should be its health; they are sins that are their own punishments, and yet not the worst that attend them. (3.) What a righteous thing it is with God to make that loathsome to men which they have inordinately lusted after. God could make them despise flesh as much as they had despised manna. <div eID="gen2875" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2876" type="x-p"/> 2. Moses objects the improbability of making good this word, <reference osisRef="Num.11.21-Num.11.22">v. 21, 22</reference>. It is an objection like that which the disciples made, <reference osisRef="Mark.8.4">Mark viii. 4</reference>, <hi type="italic">Whence can a man satisfy these men?</hi> Some excuse Moses here, and construe what he says as only a modest enquiry which way the supply must be expected; but it savours too much of diffidence and distrust of God to be justified. He objects the number of the people, as if he that provided bread for them all could not, by the same unlimited power, provide flesh, too. He reckons it must be the flesh either of beasts or fishes, because they are the most bulky animals, little thinking that the flesh of birds, little birds, should serve the purpose. God sees not as man sees, but his thoughts are above ours. He objects the greediness of the people's desires in that word, <hi type="italic">to suffice them.</hi> Note, Even true and great believers sometimes find it hard to trust God under the discouragements of second causes, and <hi type="italic">against hope to believe in hope.</hi> Moses himself could scarcely forbear saying, <hi type="italic">Can God furnish a table in the wilderness?</hi> when this had become the common cry. No doubt this was his infirmity. <div eID="gen2876" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2877" type="x-p"/> 3. God gives a short but sufficient answer to the objection in that question, <hi type="italic">Has the Lord's hand waxed short?</hi> <reference osisRef="Num.11.23">v. 23</reference>. If Moses had remembered <hi type="italic">the years of the right hand of the Most High,</hi> he would not have started all these difficulties; therefore God reminds him of them, intimating that this objection reflected upon the divine power, of which he himself had been so often, not only the witness, but the instrument. Had he forgotten what wonders the divine power had wrought for that people, when it inflicted the plagues of Egypt, divided the sea, broached the rock, and rained bread from heaven? Had that power abated? Was God weaker than he used to be? Or was he tired with what he had done? Whatever our unbelieving hearts may suggest to the contrary, it is certain, (1.) That God's hand is not short; his power cannot be restrained in the exerting of itself by any thing but his own will; with him nothing is impossible. That hand is not short which measures the waters, metes out the heavens (<reference osisRef="Isa.40.12">Isa. xl. 12</reference>), and grasps the winds, <reference osisRef="Prov.30.4">Prov. xxx. 4</reference>. (2.) That it has not waxed short. He is as strong as ever he was, <hi type="italic">fainteth not, neither is weary.</hi> And this is sufficient to silence all our distrusts when means fail us, <hi type="italic">Is any thing too hard for the Lord?</hi> God here brings Moses to this first principle, sets him back in his lesson, to learn the ancient name of God, <hi type="italic">The Lord God Almighty,</hi> and puts the proof upon the issue: <hi type="italic">Thou shalt see whether my word shall come to pass or not.</hi> This magnifies God's word above all his name, that his works never come short of it. If he speaks, it is done.
entries.a6eb5095184c63eaea9c5d3bd86a1d72d4acf7dc: <div eID="gen2877" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">God Promises the People Flesh; The Case of Eldad and Medad. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1490.)</title> <div sID="gen2878" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">24</hi> And Moses went out, and told the people the words of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and gathered the seventy men of the elders of the people, and set them round about the tabernacle. <hi type="super">25</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> came down in a cloud, and spake unto him, and took of the spirit that <hi type="italic">was</hi> upon him, and gave <hi type="italic">it</hi> unto the seventy elders: and it came to pass, <hi type="italic">that,</hi> when the spirit rested upon them, they prophesied, and did not cease. <hi type="super">26</hi> But there remained two <hi type="italic">of the</hi> men in the camp, the name of the one <hi type="italic">was</hi> Eldad, and the name of the other Medad: and the spirit rested upon them; and they <hi type="italic">were</hi> of them that were written, but went not out unto the tabernacle: and they prophesied in the camp. <hi type="super">27</hi> And there ran a young man, and told Moses, and said, Eldad and Medad do prophesy in the camp. <hi type="super">28</hi> And Joshua the son of Nun, the servant of Moses, <hi type="italic">one</hi> of his young men, answered and said, My lord Moses, forbid them. <hi type="super">29</hi> And Moses said unto him, Enviest thou for my sake? would God that all the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> 's people were prophets, <hi type="italic">and</hi> that the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> would put his spirit upon them! <hi type="super">30</hi> And Moses gat him into the camp, he and the elders of Israel. <div eID="gen2878" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2879" type="x-p"/> We have here the performance of God's word to Moses, that he should have help in the government of Israel. <div eID="gen2879" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2880" type="x-p"/> I. Here is the case of the seventy privy-counsellors in general. Moses, though a little disturbed by the tumult of the people, yet was thoroughly composed by the communion he had with God, and soon came to himself again. And according as the matter was concerted, 1. He did his part; he presented the seventy elders before the Lord, round the tabernacle (<reference osisRef="Num.11.24">v. 24</reference>), that they might there stand ready to receive the grace of God, in the place where he manifested himself, and that the people also might be witnesses of their solemn call. Note, Those that expect favour from God must humbly offer themselves and their service to him. 2. God was not wanting to do his part. <hi type="italic">He gave of his Spirit to the seventy elders</hi> (<reference osisRef="Num.11.25">v. 25</reference>), which enabled those whose capacities and education set them but on a level with their neighbours of a sudden to say and do that which was extraordinary, and which proved them to be actuated by divine inspiration: they prophesied, and did not cease all that day, and (some think) only that day. They discoursed to the people of the things of God, and perhaps commented upon the law they had lately received with admirable clearness, and fulness, and readiness, and aptness of expression, so that all who heard them might see and say that <hi type="italic">God was with them of a truth;</hi> see <reference osisRef="1Cor.14.24-1Cor.14.25">1 Cor. xiv. 24, 25</reference>. Thus, long afterwards, Saul was marked for the government by the gift of prophecy, which came upon him for a day and a night, <reference osisRef="1Sam.10.6">1 Sam. x. 6</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.10.11">11</reference>. When Moses was to fetch Israel out of Egypt, Aaron was appointed to be his prophet, <reference osisRef="Exod.7.1">Exod. vii. 1</reference>. But, now that God had called Aaron to other work, in his room Moses has seventy prophets to attend him. Note, Those are fittest to rule in God's Israel that are well acquainted with divine things and are apt to teach to edification. <div eID="gen2880" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2881" type="x-p"/> II. Here is the particular case of two of them, <hi type="italic">Eldad</hi> and <hi type="italic">Medad,</hi> probably two brothers. <div eID="gen2881" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2882" type="x-p"/> 1. They were nominated by Moses to be assistants in the government, but they <hi type="italic">went not out unto the tabernacle</hi> as the rest did, <reference osisRef="Num.11.26">v. 26</reference>. Calvin conjectures that the summons was sent them, but that it did not find them, they being somewhere out of the way; so that, though they were written, yet they were not called. Most think that they declined coming to the tabernacle out of an excess of modesty and humility; being sensible of their own weakness and unworthiness, they desired to be excused from coming into the government. Their principle was their praise, but their practice in not obeying orders was their fault. <div eID="gen2882" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2883" type="x-p"/> 2. The Spirit of God found them out in the camp, where they were hidden among the stuff, and there they prophesied, that is, they exercised their gift of praying, preaching, and praising God, in some private tent. Note, The Spirit of God is not tied to the tabernacle, but, <hi type="italic">like the wind, blows where he listeth,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.3.8">John iii. 8</reference>. <hi type="italic">Whither can we go from that Spirit?</hi> There was a special providence in it that these two should be absent, for thus it appeared that it was indeed a divine Spirit which the elders were actuated by, and that Moses gave them not that Spirit, but God himself. They modestly declined preferment, but God forced it upon them; nay, they have the honour of being <hi type="italic">named,</hi> which the rest have not: for those that humble themselves shall be exalted, and those are most fit for government who are least ambitious of it. <div eID="gen2883" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2884" type="x-p"/> 3. Information of this was given to Moses (<reference osisRef="Num.11.27">v. 27</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Eldad and Medad do prophesy in the camp;</hi> there is a conventicle in such a tent, and Eldad and Medad are holding forth there, from under the inspection and presidency of Moses, and out of the communion of the rest of the elders." Whoever the person was that brought the tidings, he seems to have looked upon it as an irregularity. <div eID="gen2884" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2885" type="x-p"/> 4. Joshua moved to have them silenced: <hi type="italic">My lord Moses, forbid them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Num.11.28">v. 28</reference>. It is probable that Joshua himself was one of the seventy, which made him the more jealous for the honour of their order. He takes it for granted that they were not under any necessitating impulse, <hi type="italic">for the spirit of the prophets is subject to the prophets,</hi> and therefore he would have them either not to prophesy at all or to come to the tabernacle and prophesy in concert with the rest. He does not desire that they should be punished for what they had done, but only restrained for the future. This motion he made from a good principle, not out of any personal dislike to Eldad and Medad, but out of an honest zeal for that which he apprehended to be the unity of the church, and concern for the honour of God and Moses. <div eID="gen2885" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2886" type="x-p"/> 5. Moses rejected the motion, and reproved him that made it (<reference osisRef="Num.11.29">v. 29</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Enviest thou for my sake?</hi> Thou knowest not what manner of spirit thou art of." Though Joshua was Moses's particular friend and confidant, though he said this out of a respect to Moses, whose honour he was very loth to see lessened by the call of those elders, yet Moses reproves him, and in him all that show such a spirit. (1.) We must not secretly grieve at the gifts, graces, and usefulness of others. It was the fault of John's disciples that they envied Christ's honour because it shaded their master's, <reference osisRef="John.3.26-John.3.36">John iii. 26</reference>, &c. (2.) We must not be transported into heats against the weaknesses and infirmities of others. Granting that Eldad and Medad were guilty of an irregularity, yet Joshua was too quick and too warm upon them. Our zeal must always be tempered with the meekness of wisdom: the righteousness of God needs not the wrath of man, <reference osisRef="Jas.1.20">Jam. i. 20</reference>. (3.) We must not make even the best and most useful men heads of a party. Paul would not have his name made use of to patronise a faction, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.12-1Cor.1.13">1 Cor. i. 12, 13</reference>. (4.) We must not be forward to condemn and silence those that differ from us, as if they did not follow Christ because they do not follow <hi type="italic">him with us,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.9.38">Mark ix. 38</reference>. Shall we reject those whom Christ has owned, or restrain any from doing good because they are not in every thing of our mind? Moses was of another spirit; so far from silencing these two, and quenching the Spirit in them, he wished <hi type="italic">all the Lord's people were prophets,</hi> that is, that he would <hi type="italic">put his Spirit upon them.</hi> Not that he would have any set up for prophets that were not duly qualified, or that he expected that the Spirit of prophecy should be made thus common; but thus he expresses the love and esteem he had for <hi type="italic">all the Lord's people,</hi> the complacency he took in the gifts of others, and how far he was from being displeased at Eldad and Medad's prophesying from under his eye. Such an excellent spirit as this blessed Paul was of, rejoicing that Christ was preached, though it was by those who therein intended to <hi type="italic">add affliction to his bonds,</hi> <reference osisRef="Phil.1.16">Phil. i. 16</reference>. We ought to be pleased that God is served and glorified, and good done, though to the lessening of our credit and the credit of our way. <div eID="gen2886" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2887" type="x-p"/> 6. The elders, now newly ordained, immediately entered upon their administration (<reference osisRef="Num.11.30">v. 30</reference>); when their call was sufficiently attested by their prophesying, they went with Moses to the camp, and applied themselves to business. Having received the gift, they <hi type="italic">ministered the same as good stewards.</hi> And now Moses was pleased that he had so many to share with him in his work and honour. And, (1.) Let the testimony of Moses be credited by those who desire to be in power, that government is a burden. It is a burden of care and trouble to those who make conscience of the duty of it; and to those who do not it will prove a heavier burden in the day of account, when they fall under the doom of the unprofitable servant that buried his talent. (2.) Let the example of Moses be imitated by those that are in power; let them not despise the advice and assistance of others, but desire it, and be thankful for it, not coveting to monopolize wisdom and power. In the multitude of counsellors there is safety.
entries.044136caa1b908d3b6ea14a7db207e82672c046c: <div eID="gen2887" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Quails. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1490.)</title> <div sID="gen2888" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">31</hi> And there went forth a wind from the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and brought quails from the sea, and let <hi type="italic">them</hi> fall by the camp, as it were a day's journey on this side, and as it were a day's journey on the other side, round about the camp, and as it were two cubits <hi type="italic">high</hi> upon the face of the earth. <hi type="super">32</hi> And the people stood up all that day, and all <hi type="italic">that</hi> night, and all the next day, and they gathered the quails: he that gathered least gathered ten homers: and they spread <hi type="italic">them</hi> all abroad for themselves round about the camp. <hi type="super">33</hi> And while the flesh <hi type="italic">was</hi> yet between their teeth, ere it was chewed, the wrath of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> was kindled against the people, and the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> smote the people with a very great plague. 34 And he called the name of that place Kibroth-hattaavah: because there they buried the people that lusted. 35 <hi type="italic">And</hi> the people journeyed from Kibroth-hattaavah unto Hazeroth; and abode at Hazeroth. <div eID="gen2888" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2889" type="x-p"/> God, having performed his promise to Moses by giving him assessors in the government, thereby proving the power he has over the spirits of men by his Spirit, he here performs his promise to the people by giving them flesh, proving thereby his power over the inferior creatures and his dominion in the kingdom of nature. Observe, 1. How the people were gratified with flesh in abundance: <hi type="italic">A wind</hi> (a south-east wind, as appears, <reference osisRef="Ps.78.26">Ps. lxxviii. 26</reference>) <hi type="italic">brought quails,</hi> <reference osisRef="Num.11.31">v. 31</reference>. It is uncertain what sort of animals they were; the psalmist calls them <hi type="italic">feathered fowl,</hi> or <hi type="italic">fowl of wing.</hi> The learned bishop Patrick inclines to agree with some modern writers, who think they were <hi type="italic">locusts,</hi> a delicious sort of food well known in those parts, the rather because they were brought with a wind, lay in heaps, and were dried in the sun for use. Whatever they were, they answered the intention, they served for a month's feast for Israel, such an indulgent Father was God to his froward family. Locusts, that had been a plague to fruitful Egypt, feeding upon the fruits, were a blessing to a barren wilderness, being themselves fed upon. 2. How greedy they were of this flesh that God sent them. They <hi type="italic">flew upon the spoil</hi> with an unsatiable appetite, not regarding what Moses had told them from God, that they would surfeit upon it, <reference osisRef="Num.11.32">v. 32</reference>. Two days and a night they were at it, gathering flesh, till every master of a family had brought home ten homers (that is, ten ass-loads) at least. David longed for the water of the well of Bethlehem, but would not drink it when he had it, because it was obtained by venturing; much more reason these Israelites had to refuse this flesh, which was obtained by murmuring, and which, they might easily perceive, by what Moses said, was given them in anger; but those that are under the power of a carnal mind will have their lusts fulfilled, though it be to the certain damage and ruin of their precious souls. 3. How dearly they paid for their feasts, when it came into the reckoning: <hi type="italic">The Lord smote them with a very great plague</hi> (<reference osisRef="Num.11.33">v. 33</reference>), some bodily disease, which probably was the effect of their surfeit, and was the death of many of them, and those, it is likely, the ringleaders in the mutiny. Note, God often grants the desires of his own people in love. He <hi type="italic">gave them their request,</hi> but <hi type="italic">sent leanness into their soul,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.16.15">Ps. xvi. 15</reference>. By all that was said to them they <hi type="italic">were not estranged from their lusts,</hi> and therefore, <hi type="italic">while the meat was in their mouths, the wrath of God came upon them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.78.30-Ps.78.31">Ps. lxxviii. 30, 31</reference>. What we inordinately desire, if we obtain it (we have reason to fear), will be some way or other a grief and cross to us. God satiated them first, and then plagued them, (1.) To save the reputation of his own power, that it might not be said, "He would not have cut them off had he been able to supply them." And, (2.) To show us the meaning of the prosperity of sinners; it is their preparation for ruin, they are fed as an ox for the slaughter. <hi type="italic">Lastly,</hi> The remembrance of this is preserved in the name given to the place, <reference osisRef="Num.11.34">v. 34</reference>. Moses called it <hi type="italic">Kibroth-hattaavah,</hi> the <hi type="italic">graves of lusters</hi> or <hi type="italic">of lust.</hi> And well it had been if these graves of Israel's lusters had proved the graves of Israel's lust: the warning was designed to be so, but it had not its due effect, for it follows (<reference osisRef="Ps.78.32">Ps. lxxviii. 32</reference>), <hi type="italic">For all this, they sinned still.</hi>  <chapter eID="Num.11"/> <div eID="gen2889" type="x-p"/>

entries.5a995d636c547221547115bae8516c5f86d462f0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1331"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 11</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Num.11.1-Num.11.35">Nu 11:1-35</reference>. Manna Loathed.</title> <div sID="gen1793" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1331"/><hi type="bold">1. When the people complained it displeased the Lord, &c.--</hi>Unaccustomed to the fatigues of travel and wandering into the depths of a desert, less mountainous but far more gloomy and desolate than that of Sinai, without any near prospect of the rich country that had been promised, they fell into a state of vehement discontent, which was vented at these irksome and fruitless journeyings. The displeasure of God was manifested against the ungrateful complainers by fire sent in an extraordinary manner. It is worthy of notice, however, that the discontent seems to have been confined to the extremities of the camp, where, in all likelihood, "the mixed multitude" [see on Ex 12:38] had their station. At the intercession of Moses, the appalling judgment ceased [Nu 11:2], and the name given to the place, "Taberah" (a burning), remained ever after a monument of national sin and punishment. (See on <reference osisRef="Num.11.34">Nu 11:34</reference>). <div eID="gen1793" type="x-p"/>
entries.b655048e95c0ab6600aa6cf9f0cd7c5fce7e0209: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1332"/><div sID="gen1794" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1332"/><hi type="bold">4. the mixed multitude that was among them fell a lusting--</hi>These consisted of Egyptians. [See on <reference osisRef="Exod.12.38">Ex 12:38</reference>.] To dream of banquets and plenty of animal food in the desert becomes a disease of the imagination; and to this excitement of the appetite no people are more liable than the natives of Egypt. But the Israelites participated in the same feelings and expressed dissatisfaction with the manna on which they had hitherto been supported, in comparison with the vegetable luxuries with which they had been regaled in Egypt. <div eID="gen1794" type="x-p"/>
entries.b40453418f911562f270d073b81ae60593de3869: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1333"/><div sID="gen1795" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1333"/><hi type="bold">5. We remember the fish, which we did eat in Egypt freely--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Exod.7.17">Ex 7:17</reference>). The people of Egypt are accustomed to an almost exclusive diet of fish, either fresh or sun-dried, during the hot season in April and May--the very season when the Israelites were travelling in this desert. Lower Egypt, where were the brick-kilns in which they were employed, afforded great facilities for obtaining fish in the Mediterranean, the lakes, and the canals of the Nile.<div eID="gen1795" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1796" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cucumbers--</hi>The Egyptian species is smooth, of a cylindrical form, and about a foot in length. It is highly esteemed by the natives and when in season is liberally partaken of, being greatly mellowed by the influence of the sun.<div eID="gen1796" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1797" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">melons--</hi>The watermelons are meant, which grow on the deep, loamy soil after the subsidence of the Nile; and as they afford a juicy and cooling fruit, all classes make use of them for food, drink, and medicine.<div eID="gen1797" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1798" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">leeks--</hi>by some said to be a species of grass cresses, which is much relished as a kind of seasoning.<div eID="gen1798" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1799" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">onions--</hi>the same as ours; but instead of being nauseous and affecting the eyes, they are sweet to the taste, good for the stomach, and form to a large extent the aliment of the laboring classes.<div eID="gen1799" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1800" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">garlic--</hi>is now nearly if not altogether extinct in Egypt although it seems to have grown anciently in great abundance. The herbs now mentioned form a diet very grateful in warm countries where vegetables and other fruits of the season are much used. We can scarcely wonder that both the Egyptian hangers-on and the general body of the Israelites, incited by their clamors, complained bitterly of the want of the refreshing viands in their toilsome wanderings. But after all their experience of the bounty and care of God, their vehement longing for the luxuries of Egypt was an impeachment of the divine arrangements; and if it was the sin that beset them in the desert, it became them more strenuously to repress a rebellious spirit, as dishonoring to God and unbecoming their relation to Him as a chosen people. <div eID="gen1800" type="x-p"/>
entries.54df4170391ec18892a8c5c325082a2cc66de42f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1334"/><div sID="gen1801" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1334"/><hi type="bold">6-9. But now ... there is nothing ... beside this manna--</hi>Daily familiarity had disgusted them with the sight and taste of the monotonous food; and, ungrateful for the heavenly gift, they longed for a change of fare. It may be noticed that the resemblance of the manna to coriander seed was not in the color, but in the size and figure; and from its comparison to bdellium, which is either a drop of white gum or a white pearl, we are enabled to form a better idea of it. Moreover, it is evident, from the process of baking into cakes, that it could not have been the natural manna of the Arabian desert, for that is too gummy or unctuous to admit of being ground into meal. In taste it is said to have been like "wafers made with honey" (<reference osisRef="Exod.16.31">Ex 16:31</reference>), and here to have the taste of fresh oil. The discrepancy in these statements is only apparent; for in the latter the manna is described in its raw state; in the former, after it was ground and baked. The minute description given here of its nature and use was designed to show the great sinfulness of the people, in being dissatisfied with such excellent food, furnished so plentifully and gratuitously. <div eID="gen1801" type="x-p"/>
entries.e835b2dbff74c612671721ec83b5eef5c404705c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1335"/><div sID="gen1802" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1335"/><hi type="bold">10-15. Moses said unto the Lord, Wherefore hast thou afflicted thy servant, &c.--</hi>It is impossible not to sympathize with his feelings although the tone and language of his remonstrances to God cannot be justified. He was in a most distressing situation--having a mighty multitude under his care, with no means of satisfying their clamorous demands. Their conduct shows how deeply they had been debased and demoralized by long oppression: while his reveals a state of mind agonized and almost overwhelmed by a sense of the undivided responsibilities of his office. <div eID="gen1802" type="x-p"/>
entries.3b0dfb33dd472be74f5526207d68aa939b3ae84a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1336"/><div sID="gen1803" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1336"/><hi type="bold">16-17. the Lord said unto Moses, Gather unto me seventy men of the elders--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Exod.3.16">Ex 3:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.5.6">5:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.24.9">24:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.18.21">18:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.18.24">24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.4.15">Le 4:15</reference>). An order of seventy was to be created, either by a selection from the existing staff of elders or by the appointment of new ones, empowered to assist him by their collective wisdom and experience in the onerous cares of government. The Jewish writers say that this was the origin of the Sanhedrin, or supreme appellate court of their nation. But there is every reason to believe that it was only a temporary expedient, adopted to meet a trying exigency. <div eID="gen1803" type="x-p"/>
entries.9a081b2ddf97dcb031e64b46dc62150f02005f2f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1338"/><div sID="gen1806" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1338"/><hi type="bold">18-20. say thou unto the people, Sanctify yourselves against to-morrow, and ye shall eat flesh--</hi>that is, "prepare yourselves," by repentance and submission, to receive to-morrow the flesh you clamor for. But it is evident that the tenor of the language implied a severe rebuke and that the blessing promised would prove a curse. <div eID="gen1806" type="x-p"/>
entries.a9e482db88096b69e09b3214776aa11406cfb995: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1339"/><div sID="gen1807" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1339"/><hi type="bold">21-23. Moses said, The people, among whom I am, are six hundred thousand ... Shall the flocks and herds be slain for them, to suffice them?--</hi>The great leader, struck with a promise so astonishing as that of suddenly furnishing, in the midst of the desert, more than two millions of people with flesh for a whole month, betrayed an incredulous spirit, surprising in one who had witnessed so many stupendous miracles. But it is probable that it was only a feeling of the moment--at all events, the incredulous doubt was uttered only to himself--and not, as afterwards, publicly and to the scandal of the people. (See on <reference osisRef="Num.20.10">Nu 20:10</reference>). It was, therefore, sharply reproved, but not punished. <div eID="gen1807" type="x-p"/>
entries.90d27561b0a70a101ac803741ce1f6b4427e373f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1340"/><div sID="gen1808" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1340"/><hi type="bold">24. Moses ... gathered the seventy men of the elders of the people, &c.--</hi>The tabernacle was chosen for the convocation, because, as it was there God manifested Himself, there His Spirit would be directly imparted--there the minds of the elders themselves would be inspired with reverential awe and their office invested with greater respect in the eyes of the people. <div eID="gen1808" type="x-p"/>
entries.e0ca2d41b5c5c92b3b94c0ef0180b74238e54816: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1341"/><div sID="gen1809" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1341"/><hi type="bold">25. when the spirit rested upon them, they prophesied, and did not cease--</hi>As those elders were constituted civil governors, their "prophesying" must be understood as meaning the performance of their civil and sacred duties by the help of those extraordinary endowments they had received; and by their not "ceasing" we understand, either that they continued to exercise their gifts uninterruptedly the first day (see <reference osisRef="1Sam.19.24">1Sa 19:24</reference>), or that these were permanent gifts, which qualified them in an eminent degree for discharging the duty of public magistrates. <div eID="gen1809" type="x-p"/>
entries.1b93ec5750cbb63335c5640d422ce47a80ad6e22: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1342"/><div sID="gen1810" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1342"/><hi type="bold">26-29. But there remained two of the men in the camp--</hi>They did not repair with the rest to the tabernacle, either from modesty in shrinking from the assumption of a public office, or being prevented by some ceremonial defilement. They, however, received the gifts of the Spirit as well as their brethren. And when Moses was urged to forbid their prophesying, his answer displayed a noble disinterestedness as well as zeal for the glory of God akin to that of our Lord (<reference osisRef="Mark.9.39">Mr 9:39</reference>). <div eID="gen1810" type="x-p"/>
entries.b34820d2b78fd6b1935f416b9d7a650faedea9eb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1343"/><div sID="gen1811" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1343"/><hi type="bold">31-35. There went forth a wind from the Lord, and brought quails from the sea, &c.--</hi>These migratory birds (see on <reference osisRef="Exod.16.13">Ex 16:13</reference>) were on their journey from Egypt, when "the wind from the Lord," an east wind (<reference osisRef="Ps.78.26">Psa 78:26</reference>) forcing them to change their course, wafted them over the Red Sea to the camp of Israel.<div eID="gen1811" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1812" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">let them fall a day's journey--</hi>If the journey of an individual is meant, this space might be thirty miles; if the inspired historian referred to the whole host, ten miles would be as far as they could march in one day in the sandy desert under a vertical sun. Assuming it to be twenty miles this immense cloud of quails (<reference osisRef="Ps.78.27">Psa 78:27</reference>) covered a space of forty miles in diameter. Others reduce it to sixteen. But it is doubtful whether the measurement be from the center or the extremities of the camp. It is evident, however, that the language describes the countless number of these quails.<div eID="gen1812" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1813" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as it were two cubits high--</hi>Some have supposed that they fell on the ground above each other to that height--a supposition which would leave a vast quantity useless as food to the Israelites, who were forbidden to eat any animal that died of itself or from which the blood was not poured out. Others think that, being exhausted with a long flight, they could not fly more than three feet above the earth, and so were easily felled or caught. A more recent explanation applies the phrase, "two cubits high," not to the accumulation of the mass, but to the size of the individual birds. Flocks of large red-legged cranes, three feet high, measuring seven feet from tip to tip, have been frequently seen on the western shores of the Gulf of Akaba, or eastern arm of the Red Sea [Stanley; Shubert]. <div eID="gen1813" type="x-p"/>

entries.9457d7bfe8630d9ce53e419a73fcbfbcea24e38e: <div eID="gen5463" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen5464" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen5465" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen5465" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen5464" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen5466" type="x-p"/> The people complain, the Lord is displeased, and many of them are consumed by fire, <reference osisRef="Num.11.1">Num 11:1</reference>. Moses intercedes for them, and the fire is quenched, <reference osisRef="Num.11.2">Num 11:2</reference>. The place is called Taberah, <reference osisRef="Num.11.3">Num 11:3</reference>. The mixed multitude long for flesh, and murmur, <reference osisRef="Num.11.4-Num.11.6">Num 11:4-6</reference>. The manna described, <reference osisRef="Num.11.7-Num.11.9">Num 11:7-9</reference>. The people weep in their tents, and the Lord is displeased, <reference osisRef="Num.11.10">Num 11:10</reference>. Moses deplores his lot in being obliged to hear and bear with all their murmurings, <reference osisRef="Num.11.11-Num.11.15">Num 11:11-15</reference>. He is commanded to bring seventy of the elders to God that he may endue them with the same spirit, and cause them to divide the burden with him, <reference osisRef="Num.11.16">Num 11:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.11.17">Num 11:17</reference>. He is also commanded to inform the people that they shall have flesh for a whole month, <reference osisRef="Num.11.18-Num.11.20">Num 11:18-20</reference>. Moses expresses his doubt of the possibility of this, <reference osisRef="Num.11.21">Num 11:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.11.22">Num 11:22</reference>. The Lord confirms his promise, <reference osisRef="Num.11.23">Num 11:23</reference>. The seventy men are brought to the tabernacle, <reference osisRef="Num.11.24">Num 11:24</reference>; and the spirit of prophecy rests upon them, <reference osisRef="Num.11.25">Num 11:25</reference>. Eldad and Medad stay in the camp and prophesy, <reference osisRef="Num.11.26">Num 11:26</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.11.27">Num 11:27</reference>. Joshua beseeches Moses to forbid them, <reference osisRef="Num.11.28">Num 11:28</reference>. Moses refuses, <reference osisRef="Num.11.29">Num 11:29</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.11.30">Num 11:30</reference>. A wind from the Lord brings quails to the camp, <reference osisRef="Num.11.31">Num 11:31</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.11.32">Num 11:32</reference>. While feeding on the flesh, a plague from the Lord falls upon them, and many of them die, <reference osisRef="Num.11.33">Num 11:33</reference>. The place is called Kibroth-hattaavah, or the graves of lust, <reference osisRef="Num.11.34">Num 11:34</reference>. They journey to Hazeroth, <reference osisRef="Num.11.35">Num 11:35</reference>. <div eID="gen5466" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5467" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen5467" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5468" type="x-p"/> And when the people complained - What the cause of this complaining was, we know not. The conjecture of St. Jerome is probable; they complained because of the length of the way. But surely no people had ever less cause for murmuring; they had God among them, and miracles of goodness were continually wrought in their behalf. <div eID="gen5468" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5469" type="x-p"/> It displeased the Lord - For his extraordinary kindness was lost on such an ungrateful and rebellious people. And his anger was kindled - Divine justice was necessarily incensed against such inexcusable conduct. <div eID="gen5469" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5470" type="x-p"/> And the fire of the Lord burnt among them - Either a supernatural fire was sent for this occasion, or the lightning was commissioned against them, or God smote them with one of those hot suffocating winds which are very common in those countries. <div eID="gen5470" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5471" type="x-p"/> And consumed - in the uttermost parts of the camp - It pervaded the whole camp, from the center to the circumference, carrying death with it to all the murmurers; for we are not to suppose that it was confined to the uttermost parts of the camp, unless we could imagine that there were none culpable any where else. If this were the same with the case mentioned <reference osisRef="Num.11.4">Num 11:4</reference>, then, as it is possible that the mixed multitude occupied the outermost parts of the camp, consequently the burning might have been confined to them.
entries.16234ec7617a3d276c3e90bf447116971e50b7cc: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen5471" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5472" type="x-p"/> The fire was quenched - Was sunk, or swallowed up, as in the margin. The plague, of whatever sort, ceased to act, and the people had respite.
entries.0b0db48635111df46d15cc4c1389d9e90cfdb6c9: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen5472" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5473" type="x-p"/> The mixed multitude - האספסף hasaphsuph, the collected or gathered people. Such as came out of Egypt with the Israelites; and are mentioned <reference osisRef="Exo.12.38">Exo 12:38</reference>. This mongrel people, who had comparatively little of the knowledge of God, feeling the difficulties and fatigues of the journey, were the first to complain; and then we find the children of Israel joined them in their complainings, and made a common cause with these demi-infidels.
entries.e638951a272d20de9e148975793e96ec671ad709: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen5473" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5474" type="x-p"/> We remember, etc. - The choice aliments which those murmurers complained of having lost by their leaving Egypt, were the following: fish, cucumbers, melons, leeks, onions, and garlic. A European may smile at such delicacies; but delicacies they were in that country. Their fish is excellent; their cucumbers and water melons highly salubrious and refreshing; and their onions, garlic, etc., exquisitely flavoured, differing as much from vegetables of the same species in these northern climes as a bad turnip does from a good apple. In short, this enumeration takes in almost all the commonly attainable delicacies in those countries.
entries.9a22deb4433ea22ec3dc6b7d129914749a7503a5: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen5474" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5475" type="x-p"/> The manna was as coriander seed - Probably this short description is added to show the iniquity of the people in murmuring, while they had so adequate a provision. But the baseness of their minds appears in every part of their conduct. About the bdellium of the ancients the learned are not agreed; and I shall not trouble the reader with conjectures. See the note on <reference osisRef="Gen.2.12">Gen 2:12</reference>. Concerning the manna, see the notes on Exodus 16 (note). <reference osisRef="Num.11.11-Num.11.15">Num 11:11-15</reference>. The complaint and remonstrance of Moses in these verses serve at once to show the deeply distressed state of his mind, and the degradation of the minds of the people. We have already seen that the slavery they had so long endured had served to debase their minds, and to render them incapable of every high and dignified sentiment, and of every generous act.
entries.0bcaa9b258bfb953277d4131daeea98dc5b93921: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen5475" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5476" type="x-p"/> I will take of the spirit which is upon thee - From this place Origen and Theodoret take occasion to compare Moses to a lamp, at which seventy others were lighted, without losing any of its brightness. To convince Moses that God had sufficiently qualified him for the work which he had given him to do, he tells him that of the gifts and graces which he has given him he will qualify seventy persons to bear the charge with him. This was probably intended as a gracious reproof. Query. Did not Moses lose a measure of his gifts in this business? And is it not right that he whom God has called to and qualified for some particular office, should lose those gifts which he either undervalues or refuses to employ for God in the way appointed? Is there not much reason to believe that many cases have occurred where the spiritual endowments of particular persons have been taken away and given to others who made a better use of them? Hence the propriety of that exhortation, <reference osisRef="Rev.3.11">Rev 3:11</reference> : Hold that fast which thou hast, that no man take thy crown. The gracious God never called a man to perform a work without furnishing him with adequate strength; and to refuse to do it on the pretense of inability is little short of rebellion against God. This institution of the seventy persons to help Moses the rabbins consider as the origin of their grand council called the Sanhedrin. But we find that a council of seventy men, elders of Israel, had existed among the people a year before this time. See <reference osisRef="Exo.24.9">Exo 24:9</reference> (note); see the advice given to Jethro to Moses, <reference osisRef="Exo.18.17">Exo 18:17</reference> (note), etc., and the notes there.
entries.4096c14e6737e92e5ef2ed6d9a0b55fbe08d542c: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen5476" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5477" type="x-p"/> Shall the flocks and the herds be slain - There is certainly a considerable measure of weakness and unbelief manifested in the complaints and questions of Moses on this occasion; but his conduct appears at the same time so very simple, honest, and affectionate, that we cannot but admire it, while we wonder that he had not stronger confidence in that God whose miracles he had so often witnessed in Egypt.
entries.9ba33814d719d4e6307d7dcb480f17d67ee2545e: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen5477" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5478" type="x-p"/> Is the Lord's hand waxed short? - Hast thou forgotten the miracles which I have already performed? or thinkest thou that my power is decreased? The power that is unlimited can never be diminished.
entries.70628e24729043b66ef0f7aa248a813a1e68e435: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen5478" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5479" type="x-p"/> When the spirit rested upon them, they prophesied - By prophesying here we are to understand their performing those civil and sacred functions for which they were qualified; exhorting the people to quiet and peaceable submission, to trust and confidence in the goodness and providence of God, would make no small part of the duties of their new office. The ideal meaning of the word נבא naba is to pray, entreat, etc. The prophet is called נביא nabi, because he prays, supplicates, in reference to God; exhorts, entreats, in reference to man. See on <reference osisRef="Gen.20.7">Gen 20:7</reference> (note).
entries.b701cc643ad272c7ed219227783f71aa55328dcf: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen5479" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5480" type="x-p"/> Eldad and Medad do prophesy, etc. - <div eID="gen5480" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5481" type="x-p"/> Eldad, they said, and Medad there, <div eID="gen5481" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5482" type="x-p"/> Irregularly bold, <div eID="gen5482" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5483" type="x-p"/> By Moses uncommission'd, dare <div eID="gen5483" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5484" type="x-p"/> A separate meeting hold! <div eID="gen5484" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5485" type="x-p"/> And still whom none but heaven will own. <div eID="gen5485" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5486" type="x-p"/> Men whom the world decry, <div eID="gen5486" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5487" type="x-p"/> Men authorized by God alone, <div eID="gen5487" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5488" type="x-p"/> Presume to prophesy!
entries.5ff03596f37556940624c66c64a4eb7f90d2d2f6: <hi type="bold">Verse 28</hi> <div eID="gen5488" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5489" type="x-p"/> My lord Moses, forbid them - <div eID="gen5489" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5490" type="x-p"/> How often have I blindly done <div eID="gen5490" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5491" type="x-p"/> What zealous Joshua did, <div eID="gen5491" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5492" type="x-p"/> Impatient to the rulers run, <div eID="gen5492" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5493" type="x-p"/> And cried, "My lords, forbid! <div eID="gen5493" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5494" type="x-p"/> Silence the schismatics, constrain <div eID="gen5494" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5495" type="x-p"/> Their thoughts with ours t' agree, <div eID="gen5495" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5496" type="x-p"/> And sacrifice the souls of men <div eID="gen5496" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5497" type="x-p"/> To idol unity!"
